newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu's authority shaken by Zairean city's fall.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's authority shaken by Zairean city's fall.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's prospects of holding onto power in Zaire looked significantly weaker on Monday, two days after rebels seized the key city of Kisangani.

The rebels tightened their grip on the country's third largest city and said they would send their leadership and "ideological instructors" to install a new administration there and explain the rebellion to the population.

The fighting in east Zaire has driven hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees into the wilderness and the U.N. refugee agency warned on Monday they faced death from starvation if aid workers were not given "full access" to them soon.
In the capital Kinshasa, Zaire's government held an emergency cabinet meeting to discuss the fall of Kisangani, the biggest setback to Mobutu in the five-month-old rebellion.
"Perhaps they will decide to negotiate now. That would be the wisest thing," one source close to the government told Reuters.
The rebels say they will not agree a ceasefire before negotiations and they insist talks must centre on Mobutu's departure.

Kinshasa residents reported sporadic gunshots overnight around the teeming capital, where rumours of an imminent coup attempt are rife. In one incident, armed men opened fire from a car in the opposition stronghold of Limete.
In France, Mobutu was in hospital for further cancer treatment but a spokesman said he could be released on Tuesday.

"He went into hospital Sunday afternoon for additional treatment and could come out tomorrow morning," spokesman Gad Cohen told Reuters. Cohen said he "totally denied" all reports that the health of Mobutu, who has ruled Africa's third largest country for 32 years, had seriously deteriorated.
This was the first time the president's aides had talked of "treatment" at the Monaco hospital. They described his previous visits there as being for routine tests.

The veteran ruler, criticised for ruining one of Africa's potentially richer countries, has spent much of his time at his luxury home in Roquebrune-Cap Martin since he underwent prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland last August.
U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata urged the warring factions to give aid workers "full access" to hundreds of thousands of Rwanda Hutu refugees facing starvation.

"The refugees are at the end of their strength. Their harrowing odyssey through the wilderness has to stop now, or many more lives will be lost," Ogata said in a statement faxed to Reuters in Nairobi from UNHCR headquarters in Geneva.

UNHCR said up to 100,000 refugees were massed on the eastern side of the Zaire river across from the town of Ubundu and tens of thousands more were somewhere between Ubundu and the former refugee camp at Tingi Tingi.

Ogata expressed hope that the rebel Alliance would abide by earlier promises not to attack the Ubundu area where the refugees were converged. She said the refugees were extremely exhausted by the months-long trek through the Zairean jungle.

UNHCR would expand its relief operation and start repatriating refugees -- who fled Rwanda after the 1994 genocide -- when it gained unimpeded access to the area, but: "They must gather some strength before we can repatriate them to Rwanda," she added.
Ogata said that further movement of refugees into the jungle west of Ubundu would cause more deaths and misery and would also make it logistically impossible for the UNHCR to assist them.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), led by Laurent Kabila, has now overrun about one fifth of Zaire.
Rebel information chief Raphael Ghenda said most of the Alliance leadership was expected to spend around a week in Kisangani before returning to their headquarters in Goma.
He said Kabila would travel to Kisangani "very soon".
The rebels plan to send over 120 instructors to Kisangani as soon as possible to spread a proclaimed ideology they say is committed to political and economic freedoms and human rights.

"We will spend several weeks training people in the ideology and showing them the differences between our own ways and those of Mobutu," said student Jacques Ntabarusha, who spent 10 days on an ideological crash course in Goma.
The rebels say their next target is Lubumbashi, capital of the mineral-rich Shaba region.
